name: Cryptoglossa variolosa
intro: I photographed two adult Cryptoglossa variolosa together on weathered wood. For a first enclosure I would pay particular attention to the ground and the refuges beneath it. The published records are strongest on habitat, defensive behavior and identification of the young.

facts.title: Documented habitat
facts.text: Arid southwestern North America, including the Sand Tank Mountains of Arizona

facts.title: Adult behavior
facts.text: Ground-dwelling, with shelter use and defensive postures documented in the genus

facts.title: Immature stages
facts.text: Described and keyed by Rolf Aalbu in his revision of the tribe

sections.title: Adults
sections.text:
I would give adults a dry walking surface and low, stable shelters they can reach from more than one side. A piece of bark placed where the beetles can be seen from the side lets me inspect a refuge without dismantling it. Aalbu described retreat into shelter and a head-down defensive posture among Cryptoglossa. An adult disturbed while cover is lifted may also become motionless. I would set the cover back gently and watch the beetle when it resumes walking.
The Sand Tank Mountains survey recorded both this species and Cryptoglossa muricata in the same Arizona mountain range. I would keep identified founders in separate groups and retain a photograph of each from above. I watched the two adults on the surface of the wood. For a laying trial I would also give them accessible soil and keep part of it undisturbed.

sections.title: Larvae
sections.text: Aalbu’s illustrated treatment includes immature C. variolosa and provides a key to the young of several closely related species. I would use that work together with the identity of the parents if a larva appeared. The most helpful details to retain are the date and location of the first larva in the enclosure, its subsequent molts, and whether an adult ultimately emerges. I have no measured incubation or pupation schedule for these beetles.
